payload.throughline: Establish molecular identity from connectivity and spatial arrangement, assign configuration with explicit conventions, interpret optical evidence without overclaiming, and connect intermolecular forces to physical properties.

Objective: Classify pairs as structural isomers, conformers, enantiomers, diastereomers, or cis–trans isomers by checking formula, connectivity, and spatial relationship in that order.
Use the prerequisite lesson’s Lewis structures and three-dimensional geometry to establish connectivity and shape before making any stereochemical comparison.
Isomers share a molecular formula. Structural isomers differ in atom connectivity; stereoisomers keep connectivity but differ in spatial arrangement.
Conformers interconvert by rotation about allowed single bonds without breaking covalent bonds. Configurational stereoisomers require bond breaking to interconvert.
Enantiomers are nonsuperimposable mirror images. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; cis–trans pairs are a familiar diastereomeric case.
Use a classification ladder: same formula? same connectivity? interconvert by rotation? mirror images? The first “no” or decisive mirror test fixes the class.
I compare atom-to-atom connections before wedges, dashes, or apparent orientation. Only after connectivity matches do I test rotational interconversion and mirror-image relationships.
Two molecules both have formula C4H10, but one is a straight four-carbon chain and the other has a three-carbon chain with a methyl branch. Their connectivity differs, so they are structural isomers.
Two drawings of butane that differ only by rotation around the central carbon–carbon single bond are conformers, not different constitutional identities.
Guided practice: compare formula and connectivity before interpreting spatial notation.
Less support: decide whether rotation alone interconverts a fresh pair.
Independent practice: apply the full classification ladder to a new description.
Boundary: rotating an entire molecule on the page does not create an isomer. A different drawing is distinct only when connectivity or non-rotational configuration differs.

Objective: Assign R/S and E/Z configurations by applying priority rules, viewing orientation, and same-side or opposite-side comparison without using mnemonic shortcuts alone.
The prior microcycle distinguished configuration from connectivity and conformation. Now use explicit priority and orientation conventions to name that configuration.
For a tetrahedral stereocenter, assign priorities by atomic number at the first point of difference. Treat multiple bonds with the standard duplicated-atom comparison.
View the lowest-priority group away. A 1→2→3 clockwise path is R and counterclockwise is S; if the lowest-priority group points toward the viewer, invert the apparent result.
For E/Z, assign the higher-priority substituent separately on each alkene carbon. High-priority groups on the same side give Z; opposite sides give E.
Use three checkpoints: priority list, viewing orientation, path or side relation. Never assign from wedge direction or group name before priorities are explicit.

I compare directly attached atoms first and move outward only through ties. I mark group 4 and decide whether it points away before tracing 1→2→3. For alkenes, I restart priority comparison on each carbon.
At a center attached to Br, OH, CH3, and H, the directly attached atoms rank Br > O > C > H. With H away, a clockwise Br→OH→CH3 path is R.
For an alkene, if the higher-priority group on the left carbon is above and the higher-priority group on the right carbon is below, the arrangement is E.
Guided practice: establish the complete priority order before tracing any path.
Less support: use the stated away/toward orientation to assign a tetrahedral center.
Independent practice: assign configuration after resolving a first-point-of-difference tie.
Boundary: clockwise on the page is not automatically R. It is R only when priority 4 is directed away from the viewer.

Objective: Interpret rotation sign and magnitude as stereochemical evidence while distinguishing enantiomer relationships, racemic cancellation, achirality, and enantiomeric excess.
R/S labels identify configuration. Polarimetry supplies separate experimental evidence; its rotation sign must not be guessed from an R or S label.
Optically active samples rotate plane-polarized light. A positive sign denotes rotation in the defined positive direction and a negative sign the opposite direction; neither sign determines R or S.
Pure enantiomers measured under the same conditions have equal-magnitude, opposite-sign specific rotations. Equal amounts cancel to zero in a racemic mixture.
Zero observed rotation does not by itself prove that no stereocenters exist: an achiral compound, a meso compound, or a racemic mixture can all yield no net rotation.
Keep identity and measurement on separate lines: configuration label, composition, measurement conditions, observed sign and magnitude. Connect them only with warranted relations.
I never translate “R” into plus or “S” into minus. I compare enantiomers under matched conditions and use magnitude ratios only when a pure-enantiomer reference is supplied.
If a pure enantiomer has specific rotation +20° under stated conditions, its pure mirror partner has −20° under those same conditions.
A sample observed at +10° relative to the +20° pure reference has 50% enantiomeric excess toward the positive-rotating enantiomer, assuming matched conditions.
Guided practice: separate rotation sign from absolute configuration before interpreting the measurement.
Less support: identify cancellation in a racemic mixture.
Independent practice: use a matched pure reference to infer enantiomeric excess.
Boundary: a zero reading is evidence of zero net rotation, not a unique proof of molecular achirality.

Objective: Identify London dispersion, permanent-dipole, and hydrogen-bonding interactions and use their relative effects to predict boiling point, vapor pressure, and solubility.
Use the prerequisite lesson’s molecular geometry and bond-dipole analysis to decide whether a molecule is polar and whether it can donate or accept hydrogen bonds.
London dispersion acts between all particles and generally grows with polarizability and contact surface. Polar molecules also exhibit permanent dipole interactions.

Hydrogen bonding requires an appropriately polarized H bonded to N, O, or F as donor and an available partner site. An acceptor without a donor cannot hydrogen-bond to an identical molecule as a donor.

For comparable molecules, stronger attractions tend to raise boiling point and lower vapor pressure. Solubility improves when solute–solvent attractions can replace the interactions disrupted during mixing.
Use a structure-to-property chain: geometry and bonds → polarity and donor/acceptor features → strongest relevant interactions → property direction.
I remember that every molecule has dispersion. I add dipole interactions only after checking net molecular polarity and add self hydrogen bonding only after finding both donor and acceptor roles.
Ethanol and dimethyl ether share a formula, but ethanol has an O–H donor and acceptor. Its stronger self-association supports a higher boiling point under comparable conditions.
Among similar nonpolar molecules, the more polarizable or less-branched structure often has stronger dispersion and a higher boiling point.
Guided practice: identify every interaction present, then name the strongest distinguishing one.
Less support: connect molecular polarity and donor/acceptor features to a property direction.
Independent practice: compare dispersion using size, polarizability, and surface contact.
Boundary: hydrogen-bond acceptor ability alone does not make a pure substance a hydrogen-bond donor. All molecules still exhibit London dispersion.
